content:
What actually happens between git push and production?

That’s what I focused on in Day 02 of my 3-Day DevOps Mini Series — CI/CD: From Push to Production.

Instead of looking at CI/CD as just a GitHub Actions workflow, I broke down the complete pipeline:

Code → Commit → Build → Test → Package → Push → Deploy → Monitor

Some of the concepts I covered today:

→ CI vs CD
→ The 8 stages of a CI/CD pipeline
→ GitHub Actions: workflows, jobs, steps, runners & actions
→ Automated builds and testing
→ Where Docker fits into CI/CD
→ Container registries like Docker Hub, ECR & GHCR
→ Dev → Staging → Production environments
→ Rolling, Blue-Green & Canary deployments
→ Secrets, environment variables & IAM permissions
→ Health checks and automated rollback
→ Monitoring after deployment

One thing that stood out to me:

A pipeline isn't successful just because the deployment finishes.

You also need to verify that the application is actually healthy — and have a rollback plan when it isn't.

The mental model I'm taking away from today:

PUSH → BUILD → TEST → PACKAGE → DEPLOY → VERIFY → MONITOR

That's what makes software delivery repeatable instead of dependent on manual steps.

Day 02/03 — CI/CD ✅

One more day to complete the series.

comment: A practical challenge often appears after deployment: keeping pipelines fast without reducing confidence. Good CI/CD design also needs observability, rollback signals, and clear ownership when failures happen.
